summary:
Anambra stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch reported in October 2016 that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Anambra lies outside the twelve states that apply Shari'a criminal law, so the federal penalties apply here in full and the death-penalty provisions for male sodomy under state Zina rules do not reach this state. Same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law at entry, carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Shari'a provisions in those twelve states criminalise same-sex acts between men and between women.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice for Nigeria, reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a in some northern states. The Act also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country. The remaining provisions stand, and LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria have no legal protections against discrimination or violence.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial recorded in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE reported in March 2025 that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation documented in April 2024 kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria's criminalisation is colonial in origin and was reinforced rather than relaxed by the 2014 Act, which is why the statutory text and the hostility it licenses are treated as separate sources of risk by those affected.

Two developments pull in opposite directions and neither is settled. A 2022 court ruling removed three sections of the 2013 Act from enforceability nationwide, while proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public were still described as a live fear for transgender Nigerians in September 2022, with no source confirming enactment.

Official response to trans-specific violence has so far produced investigation orders without charges. The Abuja police chief's call for a thorough and discreet investigation into the August 2024 killing was followed, six months later, by no suspects charged.

Placement of a transgender prisoner was left to institutional discretion rather than rule, and press coverage at sentencing treated the question of which prison to use as an open one. A later panel converted that discretion into a finding of statutory violation, but only after the sentence had been served.

Travel advice from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office functions as an external warning signal: it addresses arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation together, which is consistent with how the law is enforced rather than how it is written.
localsOnly:
Residents of Anambra live under the full federal penalty range for same-sex conduct, up to 14 years' imprisonment, with no Shari'a overlay applying in this state. The Act additionally criminalises cohabitation between same-sex partners, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation or support of gay organisations, so ordinary domestic and associational life carries exposure.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage, and no hate-crime framework available to residents who are attacked.

Police conduct toward residents perceived as gay includes extortion and physical violence, with the Lagos case of March 2025 showing a demand of 50,000 naira and a beating before release. Reporting a complaint against officers in that posture carries its own risk.

Bobrisky's case shows that a transgender resident's prison placement is decided case by case. She received the maximum six months with no fine option for four counts of naira abuse, was held in a maximum-security facility, and an October 2024 panel found that this placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender, without any reported remedy for the period already served.

Residents who organise, host or attend same-sex wedding ceremonies fall within the statute as helpers or attendees, not only as parties to the relationship.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is unresolved. The sources record fear of the proposals as at September 2022 and do not confirm their status thereafter.

The scope, appeal history and practical effect of the 2022 ruling striking Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act are not sourced here beyond the holding itself, and no source states how the remaining sections have been applied since.

Anambra-specific enforcement data is not sourced. No prosecution, arrest or police operation under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act within Anambra State is documented in this inventory, so the state-level enforcement picture rests on the national pattern rather than on local records.

Whether Anambra State has enacted any own-law provisions on gender expression, public order or dress that would bear on trans visitors is not sourced and should be verified against state legislation.

Hate-crime enhancement, victim-protection machinery and any complaint route against police extortion are not sourced for Nigeria, and their absence is not asserted here as a finding.
